lessonRef.subject: financial-literacy
lessonRef.title: Guided practice: money as a tool

objective: Learners use money as a common measure by converting invented bulk prices to per-item prices and applying the better rate to a larger order.
scenario: Tomo is a made-up fifth grader ordering supplies for a pretend club. One invented option is 12 notebooks for $8.40; another is 20 of the same notebooks for $12.00. The club needs 24 notebooks.
safetyNotes: Every amount, person, business, and account in this task is invented for practice. Nothing here refers to a real household.
Never write a real bank account, card, PIN, password, Social Security, or tax number on this sheet; the task never asks for one.
This is education, not individualized financial advice. Real money decisions belong to a trusted adult.

tasks.directions: Convert Tomo's 12-for-$8.40 option into a price for one notebook.

prompts.text: What is the price per notebook in the 12-pack?

tasks.directions: Do the same with Tomo's 20-for-$12.00 option, then compare the two per-notebook prices instead of the pack prices.

prompts.text: What is the price per notebook in the 20-pack?
Which option gives Tomo the lower price per notebook?

tasks.directions: Tomo orders all 24 notebooks at whichever per-notebook price is better, then compares that with ordering all 24 at the worse rate.

prompts.text: What do 24 notebooks cost at the better per-notebook price?
How much does that save against 24 at the higher per-notebook price?

tasks.directions: Money made two different-sized packs comparable.

prompts.text: Tomo could not compare a 12-pack with a 20-pack directly. What job did money do here that counting notebooks could not?

remediation: When a learner compares totals only, have them write both of Tomo's options as a price for exactly one notebook before any comparison is spoken aloud.
extension: Ask the learner what a 15-notebook pack would need to cost to beat Tomo's best per-notebook price.
